Welcome to **2026 PINNs Workshop** — a hands-on course building toward
a real project: physics-informed inference of unknown drivers in a 1D
vertical ocean column with shallow-water coupling, motivated by AIMS
mooring data.

Course material is **75% Julia, 25% Python**, developed in collaboration
with the [Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS)](https://www.aims.gov.au/).

## [Unit 1: Introduction](units/unit_01/unit_01.qmd)

Sets the destination. Introduces the AIMS-motivated problem the course
builds toward — physics-informed inference of unknown drivers in a 1D
vertical ocean column with shallow-water coupling — and runs a live
demo of the inverse PINN we'll re-derive together by Unit 9. Treat it
as a preview: the foundations come next, and we return to this material
at the end.

## [Unit 2: ML Foundations: From Classical to Deep](units/unit_02/unit_02.qmd)

The long route into machine learning — from supervised learning and
random forests through to deep networks, optimisers, and the autodiff
engine that drives PINNs. Random forests appear briefly as the
non-deep-learning baseline (`MLJ.jl` in Julia, `scikit-learn` in
Python); the second half covers MLPs, ResNets, optimisers, and a
`PyTorch` parallel that seeds the cross-ecosystem story.

## [Unit 3: Scientific Machine Learning and Physics-Informed Machine Learning](units/unit_03/unit_03.qmd)

A conceptual tour of the broader physics-aware ML landscape and a
first encounter with physics-informed machine learning (PIML). Hybrid
physics+ML models, surrogate solvers, conservation-aware architectures,
Hamiltonian and Lagrangian neural networks (briefly), and equation
discovery via SINDy. The unit closes with the conceptual PINN setup
that Units 5–9 then implement.

## [Unit 4: Learning Dynamics with Neural Differential Equations](units/unit_04/unit_04.qmd)

Ordinary differential equations as models of dynamics, framed through
universal approximation rather than classical numerics — no
Runge–Kutta theory, no stiff-solver internals. We follow the
ResNet-to-Neural-ODE bridge from Unit 2 and arrive at Universal
Differential Equations: known physics + learnable closure. Worked
examples include a damped pendulum with unknown friction and a
Lotka–Volterra inverse variant.

## [Unit 5: PINNs on Basic Models](units/unit_05/unit_05.qmd)

Our first hands-on PINN, in the simplest possible settings: a small
collection of ODEs (harmonic oscillator, damped pendulum, Lotka–Volterra
forward and inverse) and the simplest PDE (1D diffusion). The aim is
to make the ingredients concrete — residual loss, initial conditions
in the loss, collocation points, autodiff — and to spot a few failure
modes (spectral bias, loss imbalance, causal violation) before
tackling formal PDE theory in Unit 6 and harder PDE PINNs in Unit 7.

## [Unit 6: PDE Bootcamp](units/unit_06/unit_06.qmd)

A fast, intensive tour of the PDE essentials we'll need: classification
(elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic), boundary and initial conditions,
well-posedness, the three canonical mechanisms (diffusion, advection,
reaction), and finite-difference numerics. Closes with the linearised
shallow water equations as a worked nonlinear example we revisit in
the capstone.

## [Unit 7: When PINNs Meet PDEs](units/unit_07/unit_07.qmd)

Vanilla PINNs work on some PDEs and fail surprisingly often on
others. We diagnose the failure modes (loss imbalance, spectral bias,
causal violation) on a column heat equation and on shallow water, then
walk through the modern fixes that mostly close the gap: causal
training, Fourier feature embeddings, hard boundary-condition
enforcement, adaptive loss weighting. By the end the toolkit needed
for the capstone is in place.

## [Unit 8: The Science of Ocean PDE Modelling](units/unit_08/unit_08.qmd)

A short, intuition-first tour of the ocean physics that powers the
capstone — for people fluent in PDEs and ML but not in
oceanography. Why oceans matter, the column idealisation,
advection vs diffusion in fluids, the surface energy budget,
stratification and mixing, and the dimensionless regimes that say
which terms win on which scales. By the end the equations in
Unit 9 read as a familiar set of mechanisms in a new domain.

## [Unit 9: Project Specification](units/unit_09/unit_09.qmd)

The capstone written down concretely: the mock story, the coupled
1D-column + 2D-shallow-water model, the column equation, boundary
and initial conditions, forcing functions, reference parameters,
and the six toy tasks that build up from pure diffusion to the
forward storm scenario and the inverse problem. Implementation
lives in Unit 10.

## [Unit 10: Project Solution](units/unit_10/unit_10.qmd)

The capstone solved: a `MethodOfLines.jl` finite-difference
reference that walks through the four toy-task scenarios with
plots, a forward PINN trained against that reference, an inverse
PINN that recovers an unknown wind-stress envelope from sparse
mooring data, and a Python parallel using `DeepXDE`. Source code
embedded inline.
